newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: HILL DEFENDS COLSTON INQUIRY
The government leader in the Senate says the Government wants to have all the information on Senator Mal Colston's travel allowances, before deciding whether to take further action.
The Federal Opposition has claimed the Government's shielding Senator Colston from a police inquiry.
The Government has refused the Senate President, Margaret Reid, access to legal advice, until after a departmental inquiry is complete.
Liberal Senator Robert Hill says Attorney-General Daryl Williams will provide advice to Senator Reid "in due course", following completion of departmental inquiries.
ACCI TO EXAMINE BANK MERGER
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission says it will carefully examine a proposal for a merger between Westpac and the Bank of Melbourne.

The banks today confirmed that Westpac will offer to buy out all issued shares in the Bank of Melbourne. The Federal Treasurer, Peter Costello, says he won't decide if the merger will be allowed until the Government responds to the Wallis report into Australia's financial system.
However, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has previously said it was likely to oppose mergers, if it meant there'd be no significant regional bank left in a state.
TRADE SURPLUS CAN'T BE SUSTAINED: ECONOMIST
A market economist predicts imports will increase with extra demand this year and the current account deficit will rise.
GIO Australia Chief Economist Akis Haralabopoulos, was commenting on today's bigger than expected surplus in the trade of goods and services.

Mr Haralabopoulos says he doesn't think the turnaround from a 38 million dollar deficit in January to a 336 million dollar excess of exports over imports in February can be sustained as the economy picks up steam.
Exports of goods and services rose by six per cent, imports rose by just two per cent.
BODY MAY BE MISSING PERTH WOMAN
Members of the police Macro Taskforce investigating the disappearance of three women from Claremont are on their way to bushland north of Perth, where a body has been found.
The body was found by a person walking in the bush, inland from Alkimos, just before 11 o'clock this morning.
Police investigators and a pathologist have gone to the scene.
The sex of the body has not been determined, and at this stage it is not clear if the body is connected with the disappearance of the three women from Claremont.
Roads have been closed one kilometre back from the scene.
It's now three weeks since 27 year old Ciara Glennon went missing from the popular Continental Hotel in Claremont, sparking a massive police search.
SPECIAL SALMONELLA TASKFORCE
A special taskforce has been formed to investigate the recent outbreaks of salmonella in Victorian smallgoods.

The Don Smallgoods' products are being recalled nationally following tests by the West Australian Health Department which detected salmonella bacteria in Latvian liver spread and 'deli supreme' Kabana.
The recall follows news that 19 Victorians have been affected by salmonella traced to another Victorian company, Fabbris Smallgoods.
The taskforce team, comprising representatives from the CSIRO, Victoria University and the meat industry, hopes to determine the cause of the outbreaks and recommend preventative measures.
David Abba, from the National Meat Association, says the Victorian industry has one of the highest standards in the world and the taskforce is charged with maintaining that position.
QUINN GIVES EVIDENCE IN FRAUD TRIAL
Former Coles Myer Chief Brian Quinn is giving evidence in his fraud trial in the Supreme Court.

Quinn has pleaded not guilty to conspiring with the former head of the company's maintenance Department Graham Lanyon, to defraud Coles Myer of more than four-million dollars to pay for his house renovations.
Mr Quinn has told the court he had nothing but a working relationship with Mr Lanyon, and had never asked him to do anything dishonest on his behalf.
He described as ridiculous that he was involved in a conspiracy with Mr Lanyon.
His evidence is continuing.
NEW MEASURES TO REDUCE ROAD TOLL RECOMMENDED
There'll be a 50-kilometre an hour speed limit in urban residential areas if a recommendation from parliamentary road safety committees is taken up.

The committees unanimously supported the lower speed limit at a national summit in Sydney, ahead of a meeting of Transport ministers next month. The summit has also called on the ministers to implement alcohol ignition interlock devices, which render a vehicle inoperable, for repeat drink drivers.
The Transport ministers are expected to endorse a national road safety package to encourage consistent law-making across the country.
